newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia beef exports seen squeezed again.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia beef exports seen squeezed again.

text.p: Australian beef exports and livestock prices are expected to be constrained again in 1997 by heavy U.S. supplies and exports to Asia, the Australian Meat and Livestock Corp (AMLC) said in its Meat and Livestock Review.

But Australia should be able to increase exports to its main market, Japan, to more than the 280,000 tonnes of 1996, it said. The Japanese imported beef market should show solid growth in 1997, unlike 1996 when consumption was cut by concern over BSE and E. Coli diseases and infections, AMLC said.
Competition from U.S. exporters would again impinge on Australia's market share in Japan during 1997, AMLC said.
The USDA was forecasting U.S. beef and veal exports to increase a further 18 percent during 1997, taking total exports to 660,000 tonnes product weight.
Japan's beef imports are forecast to grow about five percent in 1997 to about 670,000 tonnes product weight, it said.
Trends would be underpinned by high U.S. cow kill rates in the first half of 1997, it said.
Improved North Asian demand and, later in the year, reduced cow slaughter from the U.S., would be positive factors for Australia in the North Asian market, it said.
"Ninteen ninety seven will be another tough year for (U.S.) feedlotters and producers," it said.
Opinion was divided on price forecasts for 1997, with some analysts expecting highs in the March-April period and others year-lows in the second quarter, the AMLC said.
But it was commonly believed that liquidation would continue, although at lower rates than in 1996, it said.
Lower corn prices would encourage greater fed beef output through increased feedlot utilisation and higher carcase weights, it said.
Cattle prices should improve in the third and fourth quarters, it said.
U.S. cattle inventories were seen declining to about 101.5 million head from 103.8 million head, it said.
Australia exported 57,600 tonnes to South Korea in 1996, down 10 percent on 1995,the AMLC said.

Positive elements in the Korean market in 1997 include an increase in the quota to 167,000 tonnes, a shift in the composition of tenders to include larger volumes of grassfed fullsets and improved consumption rates as the effects of food safety problems are overcome, it said.
But the new year would bring challenges in the Korean market, it said.

These included the increased proportion of tenders allocated to the Simultaneous-Buy-Sell portion of the market in which the U.S. is the dominant supplier, continued fierce competition from New Zealand in the grassfed portion of tenders and problems relating to larger Korean domestic production, it said.
